questions.q: What does the Markov property state about a process X_0, X_1, X_2, ...?
options: Every state must be visited exactly once
The distribution of X_{n+1} given the entire past depends only on the current state X_n
All transition probabilities must be equal
The process must eventually return to its starting state
questions.explain: The Markov property says the future is independent of the past given the present: P(X_{n+1}=j | X_n=i, X_{n-1}, ...) = P(X_{n+1}=j | X_n=i).

questions.q: Given a one-step transition matrix P, how do you compute the probability of transitioning from state i to state j over exactly n steps?
options: Multiply P by n
Take the (i,j) entry of the matrix power Pⁿ
Add P to itself n times
Take the determinant of P
questions.explain: By the Chapman-Kolmogorov equation, n-step transition probabilities are given by the matrix power Pⁿ; its (i,j) entry is the probability of being in state j after n steps starting from state i.

questions.q: What defines a stationary distribution π for a Markov chain with transition matrix P?
options: π is any arbitrary probability vector
πP = π, i.e., π is a left eigenvector of P with eigenvalue 1, normalized to sum to 1
π must assign probability 1 to a single state
π = P⁻¹
questions.explain: A stationary distribution satisfies πP = π — once the chain's distribution equals π, it remains π after another transition. This is equivalent to π being a left eigenvector of P for eigenvalue 1.

questions.q: In the credit-rating example, why doesn't a traditional stationary distribution exist among the non-default rating states?
options: Because the transition matrix isn't square
Because the Default state is absorbing, so probability mass keeps draining out of the live ratings into Default as time progresses, rather than settling into a fixed mix
Because credit ratings never change
Because the rows of P don't sum to 1
questions.explain: With an absorbing default state (P_DD = 1 and no way out), probability mass continually flows into Default over time, so there's no fixed stationary distribution among the surviving ratings — instead, default probability approaches 1 in the long run.

questions.q: Why do real-world credit risk models report finite-horizon default probabilities (e.g., 5-year or 10-year) rather than a single stationary distribution?
options: Because stationary distributions are always equal to 1
Because with an absorbing default state, the only meaningful long-run outcome is eventual default, so practitioners instead compute Pⁿ for specific, useful horizons
Because transition matrices cannot be raised to powers greater than 2
Because finite-horizon probabilities are always identical to the one-step probabilities
questions.explain: Since the chain has an absorbing default state with no competing stationary distribution among live ratings, the practically useful quantities are specific finite-horizon transition probabilities (via Pⁿ for a chosen n), not a long-run stationary mix.
